credit: Some explanations are adapted from MedlinePlus (National Library of Medicine) and HealthCare.gov; neither endorses CareCost.

xray.short: A fast, painless picture made with a small dose of radiation. Bones show up clearly, so it can reveal breaks, arthritis, bone spurs and calcium deposits. It does not show tendons or cartilage well. Usually no preparation; a radiologist reads it and sends the result to your doctor.

mri.short: A scanner that uses a strong magnet and radio waves (no X-ray radiation) to make detailed pictures of tendons, cartilage and other soft parts. You lie still inside a tube-shaped machine while it makes loud knocking sounds. Tell the staff about any metal or implants in your body first.

ultrasound.short: A handheld probe on your skin sends sound waves and turns the echoes into a moving picture. It is good at soft tissue near the surface, such as shoulder tendons. No radiation and usually no prep.

mr_arthrogram.plain_name: Detailed scan with dye in the joint
mr_arthrogram.short: First a doctor injects contrast dye into the joint (usually guided by live X-ray), then you have a detailed magnet scan. The dye spreads into small tears, so it can show damage to the rim of cartilage in the shoulder socket that a plain scan may miss. It is two procedures on one day.

steroid_injection.short: A needle puts a strong anti-inflammatory medicine, usually mixed with a numbing medicine, into or near the painful joint. It can calm pain for a while so exercise is easier; it does not repair a tear. The medicine itself is often billed as a separate line.

pt_evaluation.plain_name: First visit for a guided exercise plan
pt_evaluation.short: A licensed therapist measures your strength and movement, then builds an exercise plan. Later visits are billed separately, usually per block of minutes of treatment.

biopsy.plain_name: Taking a small sample to test
biopsy.short: The doctor numbs the area and removes a small piece of tissue, or the whole spot, so it can be checked under a microscope. For a skin spot this is done in the office with a blade (shave), a small round cutter (punch) or a scalpel (excision).

pathology.plain_name: Lab check of the sample under a microscope
pathology.short: A specialist doctor (a pathologist) studies the tissue that was removed and writes the diagnosis. It is a separate bill from the procedure, often from a different company or lab you never meet.

colonoscopy.plain_name: Camera check of the whole colon
colonoscopy.short: A thin, bendable tube with a light and camera is passed through the bottom to look at the entire large intestine. Growths can be removed during the same procedure. You need a cleanout the day before and someone to take you home.

anesthesia.plain_name: Medicine so you sleep or relax through it
anesthesia.short: Medicine given through an IV so you are very relaxed or asleep and feel no pain during a procedure. When an anesthesia team gives it, it usually arrives as its own bill.

polyp.plain_name: Small growth on the inner wall
polyp.short: A small bump of tissue on the lining of the colon. Most are harmless, but some can turn into cancer over years, which is why they are removed when found during a screening check.

upper_endoscopy.plain_name: Camera check of the food pipe and stomach
upper_endoscopy.short: A thin camera tube goes through the mouth, usually while you are sedated, to look at the food pipe, stomach and the start of the small intestine. Small tissue samples can be taken at the same time.

acid_reducer.short: A medicine that lowers how much acid the stomach makes. Some are sold over the counter. Doctors usually try it once a day before a meal for about 8 weeks before ordering tests.

rotator_cuff.plain_name: Tendons that lift and turn the arm
rotator_cuff.short: A group of four muscles and their tendons that hold the ball of the upper arm in the shoulder socket. Most problems come from wear over time, and they become more common after age 40.

labrum.plain_name: Rim of cartilage around the shoulder socket
labrum.short: A ring of firm, rubbery tissue that deepens the shallow shoulder socket and helps keep the ball in place. Tears can cause catching, clicking with pain, or a feeling that the shoulder slips.

meniscus.short: Two C-shaped pads of cartilage that cushion the knee between the thigh and shin bones. A tear can make the knee catch, lock or swell.

deductible.plain_name: What you pay before insurance pays
deductible.short: The yearly amount you pay yourself for covered care before your plan starts sharing the cost. Until you reach it, you usually pay the full negotiated price shown here.

copay.short: A set dollar amount, such as $30, that you pay for a covered service. Many plans charge it for office visits whether or not you have met your deductible; check your plan.

coinsurance.short: After your deductible is met, you pay a share of each covered bill (for example 20%) and the plan pays the rest, until you hit your yearly out-of-pocket maximum.

facility_fee.plain_name: Separate charge for the building and staff
facility_fee.short: When care happens in a hospital outpatient department or surgery center, the facility bills for the room, equipment and staff on top of the doctor's own bill. The same test in an independent office or clinic often has no separate facility charge, which is why prices differ so much.

in_network.plain_name: Doctors your plan has a deal with
in_network.short: Providers and facilities that signed a contract with your insurer. You pay the contracted price and usually much less of it than you would out of network.

bundle_price.plain_name: One price for all the pieces
bundle_price.short: A single price that covers several things that usually come as separate bills, such as the procedure, the facility, sedation and the lab. Our price is the sum of the separate pieces unless a provider publishes one combined price.

referral.plain_name: Permission slip from your main doctor
referral.short: A note from your main (primary care) doctor that sends you on to a specialist. Many HMO-type plans will not pay for the specialist visit without one, so you may need a primary-care visit first.

hmo.plain_name: Plan that keeps you inside its network
hmo.short: A plan that generally covers only doctors who work for or contract with it (except emergencies) and often needs a referral from your primary care doctor before you see a specialist.

ppo.plain_name: Plan that lets you go outside its network for more money
ppo.short: A plan with a network of preferred doctors. Staying in network costs you less; you can go out of network but pay more. Usually no referral needed to see a specialist.
